extracted.intended_audience: journalists, activists, lawyers, researchers and members of the public interested in SLAPPs and anti‑SLAPP law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and identify strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPPs), their common features, harms (chilling effect), and the statutory/procedural anti‑SLAPP mechanisms and jurisdictional variations used to detect or defeat them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of SLAPP
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawsuits intended to censor, intimidate, and silence critics by burdening them with the cost of a legal defense until they abandon their criticism or opposition. In a typical SLAPP, the plaintiff does not normally expect to win the lawsuit; the plaintiff's goals are accomplished if the defendant succumbs to fear, intimidation, mounting legal costs, or simple exhaustion and abandons the criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SLAPPs are characterized by motive (to deter message rather than obtain legal victory) and by effect (chilling of speech). They are often preceded by a legal threat and may be difficult to penalize because plaintiffs attempt to obfuscate their censorial intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum shopping
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs find courts that are more favourable towards the claims to be brought than the court in which the defendant (or sometimes plaintiffs) live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forum shopping is a common SLAPP tactic; plaintiffs may seek jurisdictions lacking anti‑SLAPP protections (for example, filing in federal court where state anti‑SLAPP protections may not apply).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of extra or spurious defendants
rubrics_metrics.description: A SLAPP may include extra or spurious defendants (such as relatives or hosts of legitimate defendants), or inclusion of plaintiffs with no real claim (such as corporations affiliated with legitimate plaintiffs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding peripheral parties raises costs, complicates defense, and increases chilling effects by broadening who must expend resources to defend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that are hard to disprove or lack written record
rubrics_metrics.description: Making claims that are very difficult to disprove or rely on no written record is a commonly mentioned element of SLAPPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous allegations or reliance on oral/undocumented assertions make defense costly and uncertain; such factual framing can intimidate critics into silence even when claims are weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ambiguous or deliberately mangled wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguous or deliberately mangled wording that lets plaintiffs make spurious allegations without fear of perjury is cited as a SLAPP characteristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate vagueness can force defendants to litigate or settle rather than risk trial exposure; courts and commentators treat this as an indicium of improper motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal, delay, or bad‑faith settlement behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal to consider any settlement (or none other than cash) and characterization of all offers to settle as insincere are listed elements of SLAPP tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using settlement posture strategically (demanding onerous terms, portraying conciliatory offers as insincere) can extend litigation and its chilling effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive and unnecessary discovery demands
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive and unnecessary demands for discovery are a commonly mentioned element of SLAPPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overbroad discovery raises litigation costs and burdens defendants and third parties, increasing the probability that critics will abandon speech rather than endure expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempts to identify anonymous or pseudonymous critics
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to identify anonymous or pseudonymous critics is a frequently cited SLAPP tactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions to unmask anonymity (subpoenas, discovery aimed at identifying posters) chill online participation and are treated as an indicator of strategic intimidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals on minor points of law and demands for broad rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals on minor points of law and demands for broad rulings when appeal is accepted on such minor points of law are tactics attributed to SLAPPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursuing appeals on technical or minor issues can prolong proceedings and increase costs, serving the strategic goal of deterrence rather than vindication of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of the suit as an indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: The timing of the suit (e.g., suits filed to coincide with critical moments in public debate or litigation aimed at delaying public participation) is mentioned as a SLAPP characteristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal targeting — suing at moments designed to suppress or delay speech or public process — is an indicium used to identify strategic motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial‑drain motive (making lawsuit as costly as possible)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some instances plaintiffs attempt to drain defendants of their financial resources by making the lawsuit as costly as possible; the plaintiff's motive may not be legal victory, but merely to waste the defendant's time and money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the observable objective is economic exhaustion rather than legal remedy, courts and commentators treat the suit as potentially strategic/intimidatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: When SLAPPs involve copyright: censorship by copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: When SLAPPs involve copyright law, they can be considered as a type of 'censorship by copyright'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using copyright claims (or threats) to silence criticism or reporting is a specific form of strategic litigation flagged by scholars and practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preceded by a legal threat
rubrics_metrics.description: A SLAPP is often preceded by a legal threat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre‑suit threatening correspondence or demand letters aimed at deterring speech are part of the factual pattern courts and advocates examine when identifying SLAPPs.

rubrics_metrics.name: SLAPPback / counter‑suits as a response
rubrics_metrics.description: In some states, defendants may be entitled to counter‑sue SLAPP plaintiffs under some circumstances; this is commonly referred to as 'SLAPPback'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdictions or cases allowing counterclaims or fee awards create a deterrent and remedy for strategic plaintiffs; the availability of SLAPPback varies by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti‑SLAPP procedural mechanism: special motion to strike/dismiss
rubrics_metrics.description: Some anti‑SLAPP laws (e.g., California Code of Civil Procedure §425.16) provide for a special motion to strike that a defendant can file at the outset of a lawsuit to strike a complaint when it arises from conduct that falls within the rights of petition or free speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such motions are designed to provide a quick and inexpensive defense early in litigation; statutes specify the kinds of petition/speech covered (e.g., communications connected to official proceedings, or speech in public forums on issues of public interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti‑SLAPP burden‑shifting: plaintiff must show likelihood of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti‑SLAPP mechanisms often function by allowing a defendant to move to dismiss on grounds that the case involves protected speech; the plaintiff then bears the burden of showing a probability that they will prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiffs fail to meet that burden, their claim may be dismissed and they may be required to pay costs and fees. Specific burdens and tests vary by statute and jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti‑SLAPP remedies and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: If an anti‑SLAPP dismissal is granted, plaintiffs may be required to pay costs and attorney's fees, and in some jurisdictions other penalties; remedies vary (for example, Ontario's law provided for dismissal with full costs but not punitive damages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability and scope of fee shifting, penalties, and deterrent awards differ across statutes and affect the law's deterrent power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of protected conduct under anti‑SLAPP statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes differ on what conduct is protected: some apply to communications made in connection with official proceedings, others to speech in a public forum about issues of public interest, or to any petition or speech about an issue of public interest (California's statute language being broad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding whether particular speech (e.g., online posts, investigative journalism, communications to government) falls within the statute is crucial; jurisdictions differ in breadth and in whether the 'right to petition' framing is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional variation in anti‑SLAPP law and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti‑SLAPP laws and protections vary widely by jurisdiction in scope, procedures and level of protection (for example, differences between California, Quebec, British Columbia, Ontario, EU directive scope, and U.S. federal/state differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because protections apply only where the law reaches, plaintiffs often forum‑shop to avoid anti‑SLAPP statutes; the EU directive (2024) and Council of Europe recommendation (2024) represent supranational steps but have material/scope limits (e.g., EU directive covers civil and commercial matters with cross‑border implications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of indicators/recommendations to identify SLAPPs
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies such as the Council of Europe provide non‑binding recommendations and a set of indicators to help identify a SLAPP, and identify types (e.g., those targeting anonymous public participation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation/indicator frameworks are tools for practitioners and policymakers to screen cases for strategic characteristics; the page notes such instruments exist though it does not list all indicators exhaustively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/right‑to‑petition yardstick
rubrics_metrics.description: Original conceptualization of SLAPPs emphasized communications made to influence governmental action (right to petition) as protected activity; the conception later broadened, and some jurisdictions apply broader or narrower definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a given communication was an attempt to petition government or was public interest speech can shape whether anti‑SLAPP protections apply; different jurisdictions treat this element differently (e.g., California broadened the scope beyond government petitioning).
